bullets: How a vector carries size and direction, and how dot products, lines and planes are built from it
slides.heading: JC H2 vectors: direction, dot products, lines and planes
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we treat a vector as an arrow with a size and a direction, and by the end you will be able to add vectors, take a dot product, write a line or a plane, and explain why sliding a vector does not change it.

bullets: Read and write vectors as arrows and as column vectors, and find a magnitude
Use the dot product, and build lines and planes from a point and direction vectors - while remembering that free vectors slide
slides.heading: What we will learn
slides.notes: Read the two goals aloud slowly and tell the class: keep these in mind, because our exit ticket at the end will ask you to do exactly these things, including spotting the sliding-vector trap.

bullets: A journey of 2 right and 3 up can start at the origin - or at the school gate, or at the top of the page
Does where the arrow starts change what the arrow is?
slides.heading: An arrow that can live anywhere
slides.notes: Ask the class: if I draw the same arrow somewhere else on the page, is it the same arrow or a new one? Take two or three answers, then say: hold that thought, because it is the key idea of the whole lesson.

bullets: A vector has magnitude (its length) and direction; the column vector records the right and up moves
A position vector is pinned to the origin; a direction vector is free and can be drawn anywhere
The dot product a . b = |a||b| cos theta measures how much of b points along a
slides.heading: One arrow, two records
slides.notes: Say this part slowly, because it is the big idea of the whole lesson: pinned versus free is the distinction everything else hangs on - position vectors are pinned to the origin, direction vectors are free.

bullets: The arrow moves 2 right and 3 up, and its column vector records exactly that: 2 over 3
The length of the arrow is the magnitude of the vector
slides.heading: A vector has size and direction
slides.notes: Point at the animation and narrate what is happening: watch the arrow move 2 right and 3 up - the column vector 2 over 3 records exactly that journey, and the arrow length is the magnitude.

bullets: To add vectors, put the tail of the second at the head of the first
The sum runs from the very first tail to the very last head
slides.heading: Adding vectors: tail to head
slides.notes: Tell them to watch vector b slide until its tail meets the head of a: the sum is the single arrow from the very first tail to the very last head.

bullets: Drop a perpendicular from the tip of b onto a: the shadow it casts is the projection
a . b = |a||b| cos theta, and a . b = 0 exactly when the vectors are perpendicular
slides.heading: The dot product measures the shadow
slides.notes: Watch the perpendicular drop from the tip of b down onto a: the shadow along a is what the dot product measures, and cos theta picks out how much of b points along a.

bullets: One point plus one direction vector draws a whole line: r = a + lambda b, with lambda sweeping every real number
A plane needs two directions, and its normal vector stands perpendicular to the whole surface
slides.heading: Lines and planes from a point and directions
slides.notes: Follow lambda as it sweeps: every value gives one point of the line. Then look at the plane diamond - two directions span it, and the normal stands perpendicular to the whole surface.

bullets: Position vectors are pinned to the origin, so every vector feels pinned
Free vectors slide: the same arrow drawn anywhere is the same vector
slides.heading: A common mistake: moving a vector changes it
slides.notes: Name the trap out loud before anyone falls into it: the arrow in the animation slides to a new start point and stays the same vector - only position vectors are pinned to the origin.

bullets: Step 1: the arrow for the vector (2, 3) moves 2 right and 3 up from the origin
Step 2: redraw exactly the same arrow at a new start point - still 2 right and 3 up, so it is the same vector
slides.heading: Worked example: the same arrow, redrawn
slides.notes: Talk through the two steps slowly and name each one as you write it; say: notice nothing about the arrow changed in step 2 - same components, same magnitude, same direction, new start point.

bullets: Add a = (2, 3) and b = (1, -1) tail to head, then find the dot product a . b
Careful - a classmate writes: Moving a vector to a new start point changes it. Explain to them why that is wrong, and what the one pinned exception is
slides.heading: Your turn: add, project, then correct
slides.notes: Give pairs two minutes, then cold-call one pair and press them on the trap: if the redrawn arrow has the same components, what exactly would have to change for it to be a different vector?

bullets: Find a magnitude, a dot product, and a point on a line from its vector equation
Explain why this claim is wrong: Moving a vector to a new start point changes it.
slides.heading: Exit ticket: show what you know
slides.notes: Collect these before anyone leaves and say: I am looking for the words free vectors slide in your last answer - if you can explain why only position vectors are pinned to the origin, you have cracked today's lesson.
